paper_title: RelateAnything: Real-Time Open-Vocabulary Relation Prediction From Any Inputs

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Open-vocabulary detection accepts any class list at inference, and promptable segmentation returns regions without class names: the taxonomy has left the model and become an input. Relation prediction has not. Scene-graph models are still trained and evaluated on the 50 or 56 predicates of one annotation style, their relation head conditioned on object labels and so tied to one detector. Three obstacles explain this, none primarily modelling: no relation corpus is both free-text and verified, a label-conditioned architecture cannot accept a vocabulary it was not trained on, and the standard metric rewards agreement with the training corpus, so a larger vocabulary scores as a regression. We present RelateAnything, a 53M-parameter model taking an image and regions from any source and returning scored relations over a predicate vocabulary supplied at inference as strings. Object labels are never an input, so the region source can change without retraining, and the vocabulary is a bank of text embeddings, not a learned classifier. It runs at 20 ms/frame. Training over 19,103 predicates requires positive-unlabeled supervision and a text encoder that separates antonyms, which contrastive encoders embed at cosine 0.95. To supply the supervision we build RA-4M, 474k images and 4.3M relations over 10,102 free-text predicates, generated against numbered box markers and geometrically verified. To measure it we build OV-SGG-Bench, six axes scored across datasets that the priors standard recall rewards cannot satisfy. On three cross-dataset benchmarks and a fourth zero-shot, RelateAnything has 2.3-3.5x the mean recall of the strongest open-vocabulary method of comparable scale, margins that survive a real detector, and leads a 3B-VLM scene-graph model on both metrics at under 2% of its parameters. In-domain measurement overstates transfer gains ~5x. Model, corpus and benchmark are public.

sections.title: Start
sections.content: RelateAnything: Real-Time Open-Vocabulary Relation Prediction From Any Inputs Maëlic Neau Independent Researcher Correspondence: maelicneau@gmail.com Open-vocabulary object detection accepts an arbitrary class list at inference, and promptable segmentation returns regions carrying no class names at all: in both, the taxonomy has left the model and become an input. Relation prediction has not made that transition. Scene-graph models are still trained and evaluated on the 50 or 56 predicates of single annotation style, with the relation head conditioned on object class labels and therefore tied to one detector and one label space. Three obstacles account for this, and they are not primarily modelling ones: no relation corpus is both free-text and verified, an architecture conditioned on labels cannot accept vocabulary it was not trained on, and the standard metric rewards agreement with the training corpus, so that enlarging the vocabulary is scored as regression. We present RelateAnything, 53M-parameter relation model that takes an image and set of regions from any source and returns scored relations over predicate vocabulary supplied at inference as list of strings. Object class labels are never an input, so the region source can be replaced without retraining, and the vocabulary is bank of text embeddings rather than learned classifier, so changing it is matrix substitution. The model runs at 20 ms per frame on single GPU. Training over 19,103 predicates requires two departures from standard practice: the supervision must be treated as positive-unlabeled, since at this vocabulary size an unannotated predicate is frequently true, and the text encoder must be corrected, since contrastive encoders embed antonyms such as above and below at cosine similarity of 0.95. To supply the supervision we build RA-4M, corpus of 474k images and 4.3M relations over 10,102 free-text predicates, generated by visionlanguage model against numbered box markers and filtered by deterministic geometric check. To make the result measurable we build OV-SGG-Bench, whose six axes are each scored across datasets and none satisfiable by the priors that standard recall rewards: frequency table over ground-truth object categories, which sees no pixels, exceeds trained model on the metric by which leaderboards are ordered. On three benchmarks evaluated cross-dataset and fourth evaluated zero-shot, RelateAnything outperforms the strongest open-vocabulary method of comparable scale, with 2.33.5 the mean recall, and the margins persist when real detector supplies the regions. Against scene-graph model built on 3B visionlanguage model it leads on both metrics on all three, at under 2% of the parameters, and trails on micro recall only when both are scored through free-text matcher. In-domain measurement overstates cross-dataset gains by approximately 5. The model, the corpus and the benchmark are publicly released. A5 is Eq. (4) at equal graph length ( 6.5). [Cheng et al., 2024, Wang et al., 2025a], and promptable segmentation returns regions carrying no class names at all [Kirillov et al., 2023, Zhao et al., 2023]. In both cases the taxonomy has left the model and become an input, which is what allows either to be pointed at domain it was not built for. Relation prediction has not made that transition yet. Scene-graph generation, the literature that would supply it, is still trained and evaluated on the 50 predicates of VG150 [Xu et al., 2017] or the 56 of PSG [Yang et al., 2022], drawn from one annotation style; its dominant architecture predicts objects and relations from shared backbone and conditions the relation head on predicted object classes [Zellers et al., 2018, Tang et al., 2019, Chen et al., 2025], which fixes the label space and excludes the region sources deployed system actually has, such as different detector, class-agnostic segmenter or human annotation; and where the vocabulary is open at all, it arrives as single caption whose predicate names are encoded jointly, which bounds it at roughly 150 strings and keeps language model in the inference path. Three obstacles have kept relation prediction at the scale of benchmark vocabulary, and none of them is primarily modelling obstacle. The first is that the supervision does not exist. Relation annotation is the most expensive and least reliable form of annotation in vision, and the machine-generated corpora that do exist either project onto fixed class list or leave the annotator unchecked (Tab. 19 in C). The second is that the architecture cannot use it: relation head conditioned on object labels inherits label space, and vocabulary encoded as one caption cannot be enlarged. The third, and the one that has received least attention, is that the measurement cannot see it. Scene-graph recall is computed against benchmark whose predicate vocabulary is also its training vocabulary, so it rewards agreement with corpus rather than the relation in the image, and model that enlarges its vocabulary is penalised for answering with string the annotation does not use. In this work, we present model, corpus and benchmark that together remove all three obstacles, and we measure the effect of each on the other two  (Fig. 1)  . relation model whose inputs are separable. We present RelateAnything, 53M-parameter relation model that takes an image and set of regions from any source and returns scored relations between pairs of those regions, over predicate vocabulary supplied at inference as list of strings  (Fig. 1)  . Two properties of that interface account for most of the design. Object class labels are never an input, at any stage, so the region source can be replaced without retraining and the model cannot inherit detectors label distribution; and the vocabulary is not learned classifier but bank of text embeddings that no learned layer transforms, so changing it is matrix substitution rather than retraining. The relation model runs at 20 ms per frame on single GPU, alongside real-time object detector [Wang et al., 2025a]. Training it over 19,103 free-text predicates, rather than the few dozen usual in this literature, changes the learning problem in two ways that must both be treated. The supervision becomes positive-unlabeled, because at this vocabulary size pair annotated riding is also, unstated, sitting on, and penalising the unstated predicate teaches the model to suppress correct answers. We address this with batch-local InfoNCE loss whose positive is the annotated predicates synonym group and whose negatives are discounted by an estimated probability, fitted on the corpuss multiply-annotated pairs, that they are also true. The target text space itself is also defective: contrastive text encoders embed antonyms such as above and below at cosine similarity of 0.95, which upper-bounds what any model regressing onto those directions can express, whoever trains it. We correct the text encoder by distilling student whose objective adds an antonym-repulsion term, so that inverse pairs separate while synonym groups stay together. Supervision without label budget. Such model requires corpus whose vocabulary is not that of benchmark and whose annotation is dense enough that unannotated pairs are rare. An image with objects contains (N 1) candidate pairs, and for most of them whether the relation holds is matter of judgement, which is why the community kept the 50 most frequent of the 36,549 predicate strings Visual Genomes annotators wrote [Krishna et al., 2017, Xu et al., 2017], and why the discarded remainder is exactly the part an open-vocabulary model is meant to serve. vision language model (VLM) is what makes the alternative affordable. We generate RA-4M, corpus of 474k images and 4.3M relations over 10,102 free-text predicates. The VLM annotates against numbered markers placed on the boxes, so that grounding is an input to the annotator rather than an inference from its output, and every proposed relation then passes deterministic geometric gate that rejects what box geometry contradicts and leaves what geometry cannot constrain unchecked and counted. On the same images and the same boxes as the annotations it replaces, the result is 1.7 denser with 107 the vocabulary. Measuring relation prediction rather than corpus agreement. Measurement has to come first, since protocol that rewards agreement with corpus cannot register whether either of the other obstacles has been removed. Scene-graph recall proves to be, to large extent, prior-matching score ( 5.2): frequency table over ground-truth object categories, given no pixels, outperforms trained model on the metric that orders leaderboards while falling well below it per predicate; the vocabulary training corpus shares with benchmark predicts recall on that benchmark; and model that learns which pairs an annotator wrote down learns the annotator rather than the image. Two scoring conventions amplify these effects ( 5.3), matcher that assigns detections to ground-truth objects without constraint and detector operating point that goes unreported yet moves attainable recall by more than the spread between published methods. Each finding constrains the design of OV-SGG-Bench. Because shared triplet mass predicts recall, every axis is scored across datasets and none of the benchmarks contributes training image, setting scene-graph generation has left largely unexplored, since results there are almost always reported in-domain [Chang et al., 2023]. Because model can profit from what an annotator chose to write down, two axes are scored against negatives that human adjudicated, on which confident false positive costs as much as miss. And because each axis can be satisfied on its own by different shortcut, whether corpus match, 3 uniform caution, collapse onto the frequent predicates or the operating point of the detector, the six are reported together and aggregated in way that penalises imbalance across them. Overview of contributions. The paper contributes (i) RelateAnything ( 3), the relation model described above, together with the objective that makes five-figure predicate vocabulary trainable; (ii) RA-4M ( 4), the first relation corpus we are aware of that is both free-text and verified against the geometry of the boxes it names; (iii) OV-SGG-Bench ( 5), the evaluation protocol and the measurements of prior and of scoring convention that motivate it; and (iv) an empirical study ( 6 to 9) organised around three questions, namely what scene-graph recall measures ( 5), whether relation prediction benefits from being coupled to object prediction ( 7), and whether in-domain measurement predicts cross-dataset transfer ( 8). On three benchmarks evaluated cross-dataset and fourth evaluated zero-shot, RelateAnything outperforms OvSGTR [Chen et al., 2025], the strongest open-vocabulary method of comparable scale, on every recall and precision metric, with mean recall higher by factor of 2.33.5 and rare-predicate recall higher by factor of 521, and the margins persist with the same structure when real detector supplies the regions. On the question of coupling we find that relation supervision sharpens object identity in the dense features without creating relational ones, and that the relation score is 8793% pair context against 0.1% object identity, so there is no shared representation to justify shared backbone. On the question of measurement we find that in-domain gains overstate cross-dataset gains by approximately 5, and that change selected in-domain can lose out of it. Model, corpus and benchmark are public. Evaluation setting. All results in this paper are obtained under cross-dataset transfer, on benchmarks the model was not trained on, with four marked exceptions: the HICO-DET row trained on 5% relation share of its training split (Tab. 4) and the three fine-tuned rows of Tab. 12. 8 shows that in-domain measurement can favour changes that reduce transfer performance.

sections.title: 2 Related work
sections.content: Scene graphs and their benchmarks. Visual relationship detection was formulated by Lu et al. [2016] as the prediction of subject, predicate, object triplets, with language prior over predicates in the method from the outset. Visual Genome [Krishna et al., 2017] supplied the annotations and the VG150 split [Xu et al., 2017] fixed the vocabulary at 150 object classes and 50 predicates. Later benchmarks changed the images or the region type more than the formulation: PSG [Yang et al., 2022] uses panoptic segments, GQA [Hudson and Manning, 2019] normalises the vocabulary, Open Images [Kuznetsova et al., 2020] is sparse and large, IndoorVG [Neau et al., 2024] targets indoor robotics, and HICO-DET [Chao et al., 2018] and SpatialSense [Yang et al., 2019] isolate humanobject interactions and adversarially collected spatial relations [Chang et al., 2023]. Haystack [Lorenz et al., 2023] differs in construction: annotated per predicate rather than per image, built on SA-1B [Kirillov et al., 2023], and alone among these in publishing explicit negatives, which is what allows 6.2 to measure precision against adjudicated negatives. Closed-set generation and its evaluation. The dominant approach predicts relations over fixed predicate set with classifier conditioned on object labels and layout, using message passing [Xu et al., 2017], sequential context [Zellers et al., 2018], tree structure [Tang et al., 2019], or knowledgerouted graphs [Chen et al., 2019]. Zellers et al. [2018] also introduced the frequency baseline that we measure in 5.2. Evaluation moved from recall at [Xu et al., 2017] to mean recall [Chen et al., 2019, Tang et al., 2019] once it became clear that the skew of VG150 allows model to score well 4 while predicting little beyond on and has, and subsequently to debiasing [Tang et al., 2020, Li et al., 2021, Gao et al., 2025], compositional augmentation [Knyazev et al., 2021] and label correction [Li et al., 2022a]. Each of these estimates its correction from training label statistics, that is, from prior of the same kind as the one it corrects. None addresses the two observations of 5.2 and 5.3, namely that benchmarks share their vocabulary with the training corpora and that the standard matcher [Tang, 2020] grants credit that object detection has disallowed since COCO [Lin et al., 2014]. From LVIS [Gupta et al., 2019] we adopt three evaluation practices: federated annotation, support-based rare/common/frequent split, and precision computed over labelled cells only. One-stage and real-time generation. SGTR [Li et al., 2022c, 2024a], RelTR [Cong et al., 2023], EGTR [Im et al., 2024] and PE-Net [Zheng et al., 2023] predict subject, object and predicate from single set of queries, and one-stage humanobject interaction detectors [Liao et al., 2020, Tamura et al., 2021] apply the same design at real-time rates. REACT [Neau et al., 2025] and REACT++ [Neau and Falomir, 2026] are, to our knowledge, the fastest published scene-graph models; both are closed-set and trained per benchmark, and 9 compares against their published numbers. All share backbone between objects and relations and condition on predicted object classes. Open-vocabulary relations. Replacing the predicate classifier with similarity against text embeddings admits new predicates at inference time. Approaches include prompting visionlanguage model [He et al., 2022], building on the visualsemantic space of grounded detector [Zhang et al., 2023], composing CLIP [Radford et al., 2021] prompts without relation training [Li et al., 2023], expanding predicates with language model [Yu et al., 2023, Chen et al., 2024a], generating the graph as sequence [Li et al., 2024b], and refining the prompting and the pairing [Liu et al., 2025, Li et al., 2025]. OvSGTR [Chen et al., 2024b] formulated fully open-vocabulary generation over both objects and predicates and defined the OvR-SGG protocol that we reproduce in 5.3. Its extension [Chen et al., 2025] pre-trains on MegaSG, machine-annotated corpus, which makes it the closest available control for supervision quality and our baseline throughout. Scene-Graph ViT [Salzmann et al., 2024] and relational pre-training [Yuan et al., 2022, 2023] learn relations and objects jointly from regiontext pairs. Our setting differs in three respects: no object class labels are used at any stage, supervision is free text over five-figure vocabulary rather than projection onto benchmarks set, and evaluation is conducted both with the answer set supplied and with it withheld ( 6.3). Detectors that accept class list at inference [Gu et al., 2022, Zhou et al., 2022, Minderer et al., 2022, Li et al., 2022b, Liu et al., 2024], including real-time ones [Cheng et al., 2024, Wang et al., 2025a], and segmenters that return class-agnostic regions [Kirillov et al., 2023, Zhao et al., 2023] are the region sources available to relation model. relation model that requires object labels can use none of them without label space it was trained on, whereas one that reads regions can use all of them ( 7.2). Machine-generated relation supervision. Existing approaches differ in how generated relation is attached to an instance and in whether the annotator is checked (Tab. 19 in C). Caption parsing [Chen et al., 2023] yields ungrounded triplets, RLIPv2 [Yuan et al., 2023] grounds parsed text with learned tagger, and GPT4SGG [Chen et al., 2023], MegaSG [Chen et al., 2025], Synthetic Visual Genome [Park et al., 2025] and the All-Seeing Project [Wang et al., 2024] prompt multimodal model directly, accepting its output or filtering it with second model. None verifies generated relation against the geometry of the boxes it names; RA-4M does ( 4), and retains every surface form rather than projecting onto class list as GQA and MegaSG do. 5 Learning at vocabulary scale. Positive-unlabeled learning [Elkan and Noto, 2008, Kiryo et al., 2017, Bekker and Davis, 2020] treats an unlabeled example as mixture of positive and negative; federated annotation [Gupta et al., 2019] is the same observation applied to benchmark. We encounter it in the training signal ( 3.3): pair annotated riding is also, implicitly, sitting on. Contrastive text spaces are known to be anisotropic [Mu and Viswanath, 2018] and to exhibit hubness [Radovanović et al., 2010, Lample et al., 2018]; relations expose an additional failure that these works do not address, namely that antonyms embed almost identically.

sections.title: 3 The RelateAnything model
sections.content: RelateAnything takes an image and set of regions and returns scored relations between pairs of regions, drawn from predicate vocabulary supplied at inference. We state the problem ( 3.1), describe the architecture ( 3.2) and discuss the two properties of the learning problem that change at vocabulary of ten thousand predicates ( 3.3); the evidence that coupling object and relation prediction does not help is separate ( 7).

sections.title:
3.3 Training with 104 predicates
Open-vocabulary relation models are usually trained on the same few dozen predicates as closed-set
models, with only the head replaced. We instead train against a bank of 19,103 free-text predicate
strings: RA-4M’s own 10,102, together with 9,001 strings taken from the vocabularies of three
further relation corpora [Park et al., 2025, Hudson and Manning, 2019, Yang et al., 2019] whose
relations we do not train on. Since nothing on the text side is learned, the bank is the answer space
rather than the supervision, and making it wider than any single source costs nothing (§ C.4). Two
properties of the learning problem change at this scale, and both must be addressed for the larger
vocabulary to be beneficial. Tab. 15 in § B summarises the notation.
sections.content: The primary objective is batch-local InfoNCE loss [van den Oord et al., 2018] over predicate slots. For each annotated pair, the positive is the annotated predicates synonym group, each member weighted by an estimated probability of synonymy and the group aggregated as weighted mean, and the negatives are the other predicates in the batch. Aligning to group rather than to single string is trade-off that we quantify in B.2: group positives transfer to unseen vocabularies, whereas exact-string positives improve within-group ranking at cost on rare predicates. Four auxiliary terms, namely per-cell sigmoid loss, swap hinge on directional predicates, background suppression and an objecttext grounding term on the pooled features, are specified in B.1, and the full recipe is given in Tab. 14. Positive-unlabeled supervision. With 50 predicates, treating every non-annotated predicate as negative is approximately correct. With ten thousand it is systematically wrong: if man, horse pair is annotated riding, then sitting on and mounted on are true but unstated, and penalising them teaches the model to suppress correct answers. This is the positive-unlabeled structure of federated annotation [Gupta et al., 2019], encountered at training time. We address it by estimating, for every ordered pair of predicates, the probability that also holds when is annotated, and by discounting each negative by that probability. The estimate is fitted on the 706k box pairs of the training mixture that carry more than one annotation, from co-annotation counts, text-space cosine and frequency, with the correction of Elkan and Noto [2008] for the fact that an unstated predicate is unlabeled rather than false. The denominator logit of negative for pair annotated becomes ℓpred(i, j, q) + log (cid:0)1 ˆP (q p)(cid:1), (3) so that predicate that is almost surely also true contributes almost nothing to the denominator; pair carrying several annotations combines their discounts as if independent. Two exemptions are essential: annotated predicates are never down-weighted, and directional inverses always receive full weight, since the supervision that separates above from below is the one signal that must not be softened. The positive-side synonym weights are an isotonic fit of the probability of synonymy against text-space cosine on 1,177 lexical synonym pairs, and the swap hinge of B.1 is weighted by the estimated probability that predicate is directional, so no semantic constant of the objective is set by hand. Direction in the text embedding space. Because the head regresses visual features onto text directions, the geometry of the text space bounds what the model can express. Contrastive text encoders fail in precisely the dimension on which relations depend: antonyms occur in near-identical contexts and are embedded almost identically. On our vocabulary the teacher encoder (dino.txt [Jose et al., 2025], 2048-d) places above and below at cosine similarity of 0.95, in front of and behind at 0.94, and to the left of and to the right of at 0.99, which is indistinguishable from its synonym pairs at 0.96 on average (Fig. 3; Tab. 16 in B.2). No visual encoder trained against such targets can reliably separate above from below. This limitation lies in the objective rather than in the visual model, and it applies to every method that scores relations against off-the-shelf text embeddings. Removing the mean direction [Mu and Viswanath, 2018] does not resolve it. We therefore distil 512-dimensional student encoder over the full CLIP BPE vocabulary [Radford et al., 2021], so that no predicate string can fall out of vocabulary. Of its five objectives ( B.2), the antonym-repulsion hinge on known inverse pairs is the one frozen teacher cannot supply, and neighbourhood-preservation term is what stops the student from buying that separation cheaply: without the latter, student reaches an equally good synonym-versus-inverse AUC at an effective dimension of 24 rather than 44. After distillation that AUC rises from 0.85 to 0.99, the mean inverse cosine falls from 0.92 to 0.09 while synonyms stay at 0.71, and hubness falls from 8.1 to 1.3. The student is used offline only; at inference the model carries the embedding bank. One consequence of this objective affects every closed-vocabulary result below. Because the model is aligned to synonym group, it frequently answers with member of the correct group other than the annotated one, for instance wearing where VG150 reads wears, which exact-string metrics count as miss. Such numbers are therefore conservative for our model, and A3 ( 6.3) provides the corrected view.

sections.title: 4 RA-4M: a verified free-text relation corpus
sections.content: The model described above requires corpus whose predicate vocabulary is not that of benchmark, whose annotation is dense enough that unannotated pairs are rare, and whose errors are of kind that can be detected. None exists, so we generated one: 474,413 images, 4,282,531 relations, 10,102 distinct free-text predicates and 9.03 relations per image, at cost of 104 GPU-hours. The pipeline, the statistics and comparison with existing machine-annotated corpora are in C. Motivation. Relation annotation is among the most expensive and least reliable forms of annotation in vision. An object box has one correct answer, whereas relation is claim about pair, of which an image with objects contains (N 1), and for most pairs whether the claim holds is matter of judgement. When Visual Genomes annotators were free to write what they saw they produced 36,549 distinct predicate strings [Krishna et al., 2017]; the community retained the 50 most frequent [Xu et al., 2017], and the discarded strings are precisely what an open-vocabulary model is intended to cover. visionlanguage model annotates no single relation better than person, but it annotates more densely and uniformly at marginal cost, and its errors are of kind geometric check can detect. We therefore use it as the annotator, not the predictor.

sections.title:
4.1 Generation and geometric verification
Generation runs an open-weight vision–language model [Gemma Team, 2026] on images with
numbered markers, one coloured dot carrying the box index at the centre of each box, so that
grounding is an input to the annotator rather than an inference from its output. Every proposed
relation then passes through a deterministic geometric gate (Alg. 1 in § C), which rejects 11.3% of raw
candidates; Fig. 14 breaks this figure down by gate. To our knowledge, no other machine-annotated
relation corpus verifies its annotator (Tab. 19).
sections.content: The design principle is that gate fires only when box geometry logically constrains the predicate. rejection is then true negative up to box-annotation error, whereas predicates geometry cannot constrain pass through unchecked and are counted as residual risk; gate that also guessed on those would replace known gap in coverage with an unknown error rate. Verification rejects relation or swaps its roles; the predicate string stays the annotators own, except in the balancing step below. After gating, 0% of containment and 0.1% of contact relations have disjoint boxes, and the corpus has no duplicate triples and no self-loops. Direction repair is the one non-rejecting gate: for left/right and above/below the roles are swapped to match the boxes and the surface form kept. Since the annotator prefers the left and upper object as subject, each verified left/right, above/below and front/behind relation is then restated from the other endpoint with probability one half, roles swapped and the predicate replaced by its inverse (to the left of becomes to the right of); the geometric top-up is balanced the same way. This leaves the corpus direction-balanced, property the model depends on and no source corpus has. The residual error classes are the geometrically unconstrained ones. Gaze is the largest: roughly 22% of looking at/watching annotations have disjoint boxes and cannot be verified. Wrong-instance grounding, prior-driven labels on very large boxes, contact predicates between overlapping but unrelated boxes (person wearing tent passes the contact gate because the boxes do overlap), and mislabelled source boxes all propagate into the corpus. One of these classes has measurable downstream effect, which we trace in H.3.

sections.title:
4.2 Statistics and training mixture
Relative to the source annotations on the same images and the same boxes, RA-4M is 1.7× denser
(9.03 versus 5.29 relations per image), has 107× the vocabulary and 1.4 nats higher predicate entropy
(Tab. 20), and reproduces 73 of the 94 source predicate classes as exact strings. Since the images
and boxes are identical, the comparison isolates the annotation schema. The distribution remains
long-tailed (the top ten predicates carry 57% of the mass), but the head predicates differ (Fig. 15 in
§ C): behind, in front of, wearing, to the right of and to the left of, spatial and balanced between inverses
by construction, replace near and on. The mean object degree rises from 1.88 to 3.20, and the share
of images whose graph forms a single connected component rises from 70.9% to 82.6%.
sections.content: holding, grasping, carrying and 535 further members of the same family are retained as distinct strings, because model whose deployment vocabulary is arbitrary must be trained on targets that populate the text space densely; canonical groups exist only within the loss and the gates ( C.4). Every evaluation split is excluded by image identity, using explicit VGCOCO id tables and perceptual near-duplicate search, which removes 8,687 corpus images and 32,456 raw Visual Genome images ( C.4). Training mixture. RA-4M is not used alone. We refer to one trained model as tower, that is, backbone, pair head and training mixture, and we evaluate two towers throughout. The zero-shot tower is trained on RA-4M together with the leakage-filtered raw Visual Genome annotations, using all of their free-text predicate strings rather than the 50 of VG150 (40,615 images, 758,547 relations, 17,742 predicate strings); the mixture is 91.9%/8.1% by image and 84.6%/15.4% by relation. This tower has seen no image from any evaluation split used in this paper and none of the benchmarks label sets; its Visual Genome share is raw free-text annotation on images outside every evaluation split. The released tower additionally includes the HICO-DET training split at 21.0% of images, which amounts to 5.0% relation share because HICO-DET annotates 1.94 relations per image against 9.02 for the leakage-filtered RA-4M, and uses the source-aware negatives of B. Its mixture is 72.7/6.3/21.0 by image and 80.6/14.4/5.0 by relation over the three sources (Tab. 14); Tab. 17 lists each share alongside the shared triplet mass it produces. Both towers are scored against the same 19,103-string predicate bank, so the zero-shot tower carries 108 of HICO-DETs 116 predicate strings as columns without having been trained on its relations. Unless row is marked zero-shot, the released tower is the model reported in every table; on HICO-DET, where it is not zero-shot, the zero-shot tower is reported alongside it. The two towers differ by less than one point on every axis other than HICO-DET itself (Tab. 29 in G).

sections.title: 5 OV-SGG-Bench: analysis of scene-graph evaluation and a cross-dataset
sections.content: protocol We analyse what scene-graph recall rewards, identifying three priors that standard architecture can exploit by construction ( 5.2) and two scoring conventions whose effect exceeds the differences they are used to measure ( 5.3), and then define the six-axis protocol on which 6 reports ( 5.4). The model and corpus of the preceding sections serve here only as measurement instruments; no finding below depends on their design.

sections.title:
5.1 Metrics and evaluation modes
R@K denotes scene-graph recall, the fraction of an image’s annotated ⟨subject, predicate, object⟩
triplets appearing among the K highest-scoring predicted triplets, averaged over images; since every
triplet counts equally, it is dominated by frequent predicates. mR@K is the mean of the per-predicate
R@K values, so a rare predicate contributes as much as on; F1@K is their harmonic mean; wR@K
weights each predicate’s recall by the logarithm of its inverse frequency in the evaluated split; and
the rare, common and frequent buckets partition predicates by annotation count in that split (below
50, 50 to 500, above 500), following LVIS [Gupta et al., 2019]. Federated average precision (fAP)
and P-AUC are computed over labelled cells only and used on A2 alone (§ 6.2).
sections.content: Under graph-constrained scoring each subjectobject pair contributes only its highest-scoring predicate to the slots, whereas unconstrained scoring lets one pair occupy several; the difference is 11.6 R@50 on VG150 and 19.0 on PSG for our model. All numbers in this paper are graphconstrained, as are the baselines. Results come in one of two modes: with ground-truth boxes the regions are given and only the relations are scored, whereas in detection mode (SGDet) they come from detector, so the score also reflects detector recall, an unreported free parameter ( 5.3).

sections.title:
5.2 Three priors rewarded by recall
Shared triplet mass. The VG150 test split uses the same 50 predicate strings as its training split,
so a VG150-trained model encounters no vocabulary novelty at all; nevertheless, open-vocabulary
methods are ranked on exactly this number on the OvR-SGG leaderboard [Chen et al., 2024b],
which we reproduce in § 6.7. We quantify this confound as the shared triplet mass, the fraction of a
corpus’s relation instances whose ⟨subject category, predicate, object category⟩ triple the benchmark
also annotates (Tab. 17 in § C). The triple rather than the predicate, because a predicate string is
not an annotation: on between a person and a horse and on between a book and a table are different
acts, and two corpora can agree on the string while never agreeing on the pair it is asserted of.
Our mixture shares 53.4% of its mass with VG150 on the predicate alone and 12.8% on the triple.
No image and no annotation is shared; leakage is excluded separately by image identity (§ C.4).
The confound is concentrated in-domain and is very large there: the baseline’s fine-tuning corpus
reproduces 90.9% of its relation mass as triples VG150 also annotates, against our 12.8%, whereas
on PSG it sits at 8.6% against our 10.7%. Because the triple charges for the two object names
as well, it also charges for taxonomy and domain mismatch, and Tab. 18 prints the components
separately. The statistic is predictive. An arm trained with a larger share of raw Visual Genome
reached 54.3 R@50 on VG150, the best zero-shot figure we are aware of, while being the worst
model we trained on every tail metric.
sections.content: Object-category prior. It has been known since Zellers et al. [2018] that lookup table over object category pairs is strong scene-graph baseline. Tab. 1 shows its advantage to be confined to the metric by which methods are usually ranked: in per-edge top-1 accuracy the frequency baseline exceeds our trained model by 15% on all three benchmarks, while on the per-predicate average of the same predictions our model exceeds it by 2986%. The baseline returns each category pairs majority predicate, which micro metric rewards and macro metric penalises. Two readings should be avoided. The table does not show that visual input is unnecessary, since the edge-by-edge join (Fig. 20 in E) finds the model correct where the baseline is wrong on 6.912.8% of edges; nor that our model is weak, since the baseline receives oracle object categories we never see. Annotation propensity. The third prior lies in what the annotation omits. few pairs per image are annotated and the rest left empty, but an empty pair is not negative one: on PSG test at its maximum-F1 threshold, 78% of the edges RelateAnything checkpoint emits fall on pairs the corpus never annotated in either direction, against 11% matching an annotated triple ( D.5). model trained to predict which pairs carry annotations therefore learns annotation propensity, which on these corpora reduces to contact prior. Our architecture contains such term by construction, the pair-relatedness score of 3.2, so its contribution can be measured, and its sign differs by benchmark family: retaining it improves recall on the annotation-derived benchmarks and degrades truth judgement on the adjudicated negatives of SpatialSense ( D.3 in D). Recall against sparse annotation and truth judgement against adjudicated negatives are therefore different quantities. protocol that is robust to these three priors should report vector of measurements rather than single number, state the shared triplet mass behind every recall cell, and include at least one axis scored against adjudicated negatives and one that frequency prior cannot help.

sections.title:
5.3 Two scoring conventions with effects larger than those measured
Whereas § 5.2 concerned what the benchmarks ask, this section concerns how they score. We
encountered both conventions while reproducing OvR-SGG [Chen et al., 2024b], the open-vocabulary
relation leaderboard, which holds 15 of the 50 VG150 predicates out of training and scores in detection
mode. The reproduction is faithful: running the released checkpoints through our inference code
and scoring them with a transcription of the baseline’s metric recovers all twelve published numbers
to within 0.35 points (Tab. 24 in § D.7). The observations below concern the protocol itself.
sections.content: Duplicate credit in the matcher. The standard detection-mode matcher, inherited from the reference implementation [Zellers et al., 2018, Tang, 2020] and still used by current open-vocabulary methods, credits predicted triplet when its subject and object boxes each reach IoU 0.5 with the corresponding ground-truth boxes and the label triple matches. No assignment constraint is enforced, so ground-truth object covered by detections offers opportunities to recover the same relation; on VG150 test, each recovered ground-truth box is covered by 2.99 detections on average. Object detection has not permitted this since COCO [Lin et al., 2014], where each ground-truth instance may be matched by at most one detection and the remainder count as false positives. Restoring the constraint reduces the published models R@50 by 12.0% and its novel R@50 by 13.5%, consistently across both released checkpoints. This amounts to 2.45 points of Base+Novel R@50, 13 Figure 4 The pair-recall ceiling as function of the detector operating point. One curve per detector and benchmark, weights fixed, swept over confidence threshold and box cap; markers are the two operating points of Tab. 23 ( D). The 4.3-point spread between all published OvR-SGG methods fits inside the vertical extent of any single curve. The baselines GroundingDINO [Liu et al., 2024] retains every non-background query, the source of its apparent advantage. compared with the 2.39 points gained by upgrading the same methods backbone from Swin-T to Swin-B, which constitutes separate leaderboard entry. The correction applied here is the most generous available, matching each ground-truth object to the highest-IoU detection of the correct class; class-agnostic assignment costs more (25.5 down to 15.2 R@50). Detector operating point. Detection-mode recall is bounded above by pair recall, the fraction of ground-truth relations for which both endpoints are detected. Pair recall is quadratic in object recall, bounds every model evaluated on the same boxes identically, and depends not on the detector itself but on its confidence threshold and box cap, parameters that are rarely reported. Holding the detector weights fixed and varying only these two settings moves the ceiling by 1249% relative across four detector/benchmark combinations  (Fig. 4)  ; on VG150 the change is 19 points, against 4.3-point spread between all published methods on the leaderboard. threshold can also invert comparison between detector families. The baselines GroundingDINO [Liu et al., 2024] appears stronger than YOLO detector, with ceiling of 0.82 against 0.64, because it applies no threshold and retains 97 boxes per image against the YOLO detectors 27; at matched budget the YOLO detector reaches 0.83. Our own A4 is measured at confidence threshold of 0.05 against ceiling of 0.696, whereas the same detector reaches 0.876 at matched budget. Detection-mode results should therefore state the matcher, the detector operating point and the resulting pair-recall ceiling; 10 lists the reporting practices this implies.

sections.title:
6.2 A2: precision on adjudicated negatives
Recall does not penalise hallucination. Since an unlabelled pair is not a negative pair, a model can
assert false relations at no cost in recall. A2 addresses this by scoring against negatives that an
annotator adjudicated rather than negatives assumed by the protocol.
sections.content: A2 is evaluated on Haystack [Lorenz et al., 2023], the only scene-graph test set we are aware of that publishes explicit negatives, that is, cells an annotator inspected and marked as not carrying the predicate, as distinct from cells left blank. Annotating per predicate rather than per image reaches rare classes that the PSG test split barely contains and makes its positives sparse: 2,870 positives against 23,174 explicit negatives over 11,368 images. It reuses PSGs 56 predicates and panoptic format, so model runs on it unchanged, and its images come from SA-1B [Kirillov et al., 2023], so it shares no images or annotation ancestry with VG150, IndoorVG, PSG or the Visual Genome component of our mixture. Scoring is federated in the sense of LVIS [Gupta et al., 2019], over the 26,044 labelled cells only, on ground-truth boxes; we report Haystacks own per-predicate ROC-AUC (P-AUC) together with federated AP that ranks within each predicate. The results are given in Tab. 6. RelateAnything improves mean federated AP by 39% and rare-predicate fAP by 59%, over 55 predicates with support of at least five, 31 of which are rare, and raises P-AUC from 83.9 to 93.7. Both models express all 56 predicates, but reach different fractions of the cells. The baseline scores every ordered pair; our relatedness sampler reaches 89.0% of the 26,044 labelled cells, and we do not force the rest through it, since an unsampled pair is one the deployed system emits nothing for. Those cells are scored zero: correct rejection for negative, miss for positive. 6.3 A3: the full vocabulary with the answer set withheld
A1 supplies the benchmark’s vocabulary to the model, which a deployed open-vocabulary model does
not have. A3 removes this assistance: the model answers from its full 19,103-string vocabulary and
is scored with synonym-tolerant matching. Recall does not collapse (56.0 R@50 on VG150, against

among 19,103 candidates is 1 on VG150 and IndoorVG and 10 on PSG (Tab. 6).
sections.content: Applicability to the baseline. For a single backbone to serve both tasks, relation supervision would have to induce features that

Querying from subjects patches and measuring cosine similarity across the image, we find that fine-tuning raises class selectivity from 0.242 to 0.281 and leaves relation selectivity essentially unchanged, from 0.133 to 0.138. Fine-tuning on relations thus made the dense features less able to distinguish partner from an arbitrary object of the same category. sections.content: Summary. Relation supervision does not create relational features ( 7.3), the relation logit does not depend on object identity ( 7.4), and object labels supply prior that inflates the metric by which methods are ranked and does not transfer ( 5.2, 7.1). There is thus no shared representation that would justify shared backbone, and there is measurable cost to the shared input. The detector can consequently be replaced without retraining the relation model, and the relation model cannot inherit the detectors label distribution.

sections.title: 10 Discussion and limitations
sections.content: Held-out concepts. Every unmarked result is cross-dataset: the images, object distribution and annotation style of each benchmark are unseen. The predicate strings are not: every benchmark predicate occurs in the training vocabulary. 6.7 evaluates the held-out variant on the split that defines it; the general variant, holding concepts out across all four benchmarks, has not been run, although the architecture permits it since the predicate matrix is never learned. Several conclusions rest on one seed; difference within the 1.3% noise floor of is named as such. 29 Corpus precision. Every precision claim about RA-4M is structural: the gate rejects 11.3% of candidates, rejection is true negative up to box error, and predicates geometry cannot constrain are named and counted rather than checked ( 4.1). We have no human-audited precision estimate, sample of generated relations read and scored by person. That is the measurement reader should expect before relying on 4.3M machine-generated annotations, and the one to add first. Scope of the decoupling result. 7 shows that our relation supervision does not produce relational dense features, not that none could: nothing in our recipe provides patch-level relational objective, which the probes suggest is what shared backbone would require. The A5 verdicts. A5 is scored by Eq. (4), the information in the relations visionlanguage judge accepts, and our model leads on it. The same judge returns two verdicts favouring the baseline ( 6.5): shown whole graphs at deployed length it prefers the baselines, and shown one relation at time it accepts slightly more, which second judge repeats ( D.8). Per-relation precision is genuine shortcoming: at any depth the baseline overreaches less, and deployment that cannot tolerate false edge should prefer shorter graph. Methodologically, judge cannot perceive repetition, so informativeness must be measured against reference distribution, not elicited. Detector recall. The dominant loss between benchmark number and deployed system is objectdetector recall: pair recall is quadratic in object recall and no relation model can exceed it, while larger relation model buys accuracy in part of the ranking deployment never emits ( G.1). Reporting practices. Each of these is inexpensive and changed conclusion here: the shared triplet mass between corpus and benchmark, beside every recall number ( 5.2); the matcher and whether it enforces one-to-one assignment; the detectors threshold and box cap, with their pair-recall ceiling ( 5.3); whether recall is graph-constrained; and one axis on adjudicated negatives ( 5.4).

sections.title: 11 Conclusion
sections.content: Detection and segmentation became taxonomy-free; relation prediction did not. We have argued that the obstacles were the supervision, the architecture and the measurement, and we have removed one of each. RA-4M supplies 4.3M relations over 10,102 free-text predicates, verified against the geometry of the boxes they name. RelateAnything takes regions from any source and vocabulary supplied at inference, and on three benchmarks evaluated cross-dataset and fourth evaluated zero-shot it exceeds the strongest open-vocabulary method of comparable scale by 2.33.5 in mean recall, at 20 ms per frame. OV-SGG-Bench scores six axes across datasets that no prior can satisfy. The measurement obstacle is the most consequential, because it is invisible from inside the standard protocol. Scene-graph recall as currently reported is largely prior-matching score: pixel-free frequency table wins the leaderboard metric, benchmarks share the training corpuss annotation style, and scoring conventions move results by more than the differences between methods. Two further findings follow from measuring across datasets. Coupling object and relation prediction has no representational basis in our probes, since relation supervision sharpens object identity without creating relational features and the relation score is almost entirely determined by pair context. And in-domain measurement overstates transfer gains by about 5 and can favour changes that reduce transfer. Corpus, model and protocol are public. The cheapest practice we recommend is to report the shared triplet mass between corpus and benchmark beside each recall number: how much of models supervision asserts the same relations, of the same kinds of object, as the benchmark.

sections.content: A.1 Visual path The backbone, the feature taps and the pooling are specified in 3.2. Two choices there were settled by ablation ( H). The three taps are layer-normalised individually; without this the fusion is dominated by the larger activation scale of the last layer. The backbone is fully fine-tuned at learning rate 8 below the heads, which at this scale outperforms both frozen backbone and LoRA adapters [Hu et al., 2022], although the ordering of those two alternatives depends on the checkpoint selection rule and inverts under best-epoch selection. A.2 Deformable scene read The read samples 8 heads 4 points around each of pairs four anchors. Three properties of the stage matter. It is additive behind zero-initialised gate, so that training starts from the model without it and the gates own gradient decides whether the read is used; module that perturbed an already converged system would measure the perturbation rather than the mechanism. B.2.1 The distillation objective The student of 3.3 is trained against the frozen teacher under six terms. Relational distillation matches the students pairwise-cosine matrix to the teachers over each minibatch; being defined on cosines it is independent of the two dimensionalities, and it is what the downstream synonym and inverse masks read. An absolute anchor, at small weight, regresses the student onto principal-component projection of the teacher target and fixes the global frame. Neighbourhood preservation is row-wise KL divergence between the teachers and the students softmax over batch similarities. Antonym repulsion is hinge pushing the cosine of known inverse pair below margin, and synonym cohesion hinge holding canonical-group pairs above one; softer hinge at lower margin holds modified spatial forms such as far above near their base predicate without merging them. The teacher targets are de-hubbed before distillation by removing their three leading principal directions [Mu and Viswanath, 2018], without which every off-diagonal cosine sits near 0.80 and the relational term is dominated by that bulk. Two of the six terms carry the result (Tab. 16). Antonym repulsion is the term frozen teacher cannot supply, since the teacher places to the left of and to the right of at 0.99 and does not separate inverses from synonyms at all (0.92 against 0.96). Neighbourhood preservation is what prevents the student from buying that separation cheaply: without it, student reaches an equally good synonym-versus-inverse AUC (0.980 against 0.989) but collapses to an effective dimension of 24 rather than 44, and its nearest neighbour lies in its own synonym group for 18% of predicates rather than 29%. The shipped student places inverses near orthogonal (0.09) while holding synonyms together at 0.71. B.2.2 Alignment to synonym group The objective of 3.3 aligns pair embedding to region of the text space, the synonym group of the annotated predicate, rather than to single point. The cost is that the model frequently answers with member of the correct group other than the annotated one, which exact-string metrics count as miss. Training against the group as whole pushes the non-winning surface forms to ranks 90338, and the surviving form is not necessarily the annotated one. The failure is easily misdiagnosed as directional one. Fig. 12 shows the substitutions on PSG. Directional strings are the clearest case: the model answers on the right of where an annotation reads to the right of, which exact-string recall counts as miss, whereas measuring direction directly by subjectobject swap places the models directional accuracy at 0.97. Every closed-vocabulary number in this paper uses exact matching and is therefore conservative for our model in way that it is not for closed-vocabulary baselines; A3 gives the corrected view. sections.title: C Corpus details
sections.content: C.1 Source images and generation We annotate the image set of the MegaSG release [Chen et al., 2025], 500k COCO-style images drawn from COCO, Objects365 and web sources, taking its object boxes verbatim and replacing its relation annotations entirely. Fixing the box set isolates the contribution of relation supervision and lets every generated graph be joined back to the source annotations for inspection  (Fig. 16)  . Of the 499,388 images with at least two boxes, 474,420 form the training split and 24,968 the validation split; seven training images lose every candidate to the gates, which is why Tab. 20 counts 474,413. Generation uses an open-weight visionlanguage model [Gemma Team, 2026] (26B parameters, mixture-of-experts, 4B active per token) served with vLLM [Kwon et al., 2023], in three passes per image  (Fig. 13)  . The image is presented with numbered marker at the centre of each object box, so that the model refers to instances rather than to categories. The semantic pass proposes actions and interactions with fully open vocabulary and an explicit prohibition on spatial predicates; its prompt ( J) is written for coverage rather than precision. The grow pass runs one additive round on the same image to fill sparse graphs; it contributes most of the corpuss density and most of its errors, and the body-part gate exists because of it, its characteristic failure being man wearing human nose. The spatial pass proposes layout relations under an open prompt that asks for depth, contact and proximity ahead of the left/right relations that dominate purely geometric annotation; every proposal is checked against box geometry, and proposals whose predicate does not reduce to one of 21 layout forms (left/right, above/below, front/behind, inside, near and thirteen contact phrasings) are dropped, since actions belong to the semantic passes. Images that remain below spatial-density floor receive salience-ranked geometric top-up, which contributes 18.4% of spatial relations. Two design comparisons contradicted the expected outcome. verify-before-assert prompt, which asks the model to justify each relation before emitting it, was evaluated on fixed 1,000-image calibration sample and rejected: it raised precision by reducing semantic predicate diversity from 42 404 distinct types to 135, whereas the deterministic gates reach the same precision at no cost in diversity. Conversely, purely geometric spatial layer was free but monotone (6 surface forms, 58% left/right, almost no depth), whereas propose-then-verify yields 20 surface forms at 32.5% depth, 29% left/right, 14% proximity and 13% contact, with left/right and front/behind balanced to within 0.4% at full scale. C.2 Verification gate Figure 14 Candidates rejected by each gate over the full generation run. Contact predicates on disjoint boxes dominate; the direction gate is the one that repairs rather than rejects. C.3 Statistics and comparison The use of models to write relation annotations is not new (Tab. 19), and existing approaches differ chiefly in how relation is grounded. The earliest parses image captions with language scene parser, which yields triplets that are ungrounded, since the parser cannot determine which of four chairs the caption refers to, and that inherit caption bias [Chen et al., 2023]. RLIPv2 [Yuan et al., 2023] scales this to 1.9M images by generating captions with BLIP and assigning the parsed relation texts to region pairs with learned tagger, so that grounding becomes prediction of the same kind the downstream model is expected to learn and tagger errors are indistinguishable from supervision. GPT4SGG [Chen et al., 2023] and MegaSG [Chen et al., 2025] instead prompt multimodal model directly, on 113k COCO images and 1M images respectively, which grounds relations in the image but accepts the models output without verification. In rankfrequency, RA-4M lies between the 94-class closed vocabulary of its source and the 36,549 unconstrained strings of raw Visual Genome: it has long free-text tail of 4,505 hapax predicates, but an order of magnitude more mass in ranks 10100, which is where non-generic but learnable predicates are found. The reason is that model whose deployment vocabulary is arbitrary must be trained on targets that populate the text space densely: collapsing grasping onto holding at annotation time teaches the model that grasping does not exist. sections.title: D Protocol details
sections.content: D.1 Relation score The deployed relation score is = σ(cid:0)a (ℓpred + ℓpair) + b(cid:1), in which the pair-relatedness logit ℓpair is fused additively; one definition is shared by the evaluator and the deployed pipeline. Additive and multiplicative fusion rank differently. The annotationderived benchmarks favour the multiplicative form, because multiplication up-weights ℓpair, the annotation-propensity term; on adjudicated negatives the ordering inverts (additive 0.911 AUC, multiplicative 0.904, relatedness alone 0.748). We report the additive form throughout. (6) D.2 Sensitivity of the composite Table 21 Leave-one-axis-out analysis of the composite. The ordering of the two systems does not depend on any single axis, including A5, whose scoring 6.5 discusses at greatest length. Withholding A4 narrows the gap most, because A4 is the axis on which the baseline is furthest behind. D.3 Annotation propensity in the score The pair-relatedness score of 3.2 is the annotation-propensity term of 5.2. It is present by construction, so its contribution can be measured on both benchmark families, and its sign differs between them. On the annotation-derived benchmarks, retaining it improves recall. On adjudicated negatives, removing it at evaluation time improves the result: every projective predicate gains between +0.03 and +0.05 AUC and only the two contact predicates lose, which is the expected behaviour of contact prior  (Fig. 17)  . Recall against sparse annotation and truth judgement against adjudicated negatives are therefore different quantities, and one term can improve the first while degrading the second. D.4 Calibration The model ranks well but on an uncalibrated scale  (Fig. 18)  . Its logit scale and bias are trained against mass-balanced objective, that is, an implicit 50/50 prior, whereas real frame is 0.24% positive, so scores accumulate near 1 and threshold has no fixed meaning; the ranking behind those scores nonetheless separates the top decile from the bottom by three orders of magnitude in 48 Figure 17 Effect of the relatedness term on adjudicated spatial negatives. The pooled AUC moves by 0.005 and reflects none of this. The probe uses the zero-shot tower, so its pooled AUC differs from the 0.675 that 6.6 reports for the released tower. What the fit is made against determines what the number means. Fitted on annotation hits, the score estimates the probability that relation appears in an annotation and reaches an ECE of 0.004 under the same protocol. D.8.1 Per-relation oracle (A5b) The pairwise oracle returns one verdict per pair of graphs and so cannot indicate whether losing graph lost because its additional relations were false or because the judge prefers shorter text. A5b scores each asserted relation separately: the judge sees one relation at time and answers whether the claim is true of the photograph. Rendering. Two renderings were evaluated. The plain rendering presents the judge with the same numbered image used by the pairwise oracle, carrying up to hundred identically coloured boxes; the highlighted rendering draws separate image per relation with the subject and object boxes in different colours. Which is better is decided by the control: fixed share of judged relations have their predicate replaced by another drawn from the same image, and the run reports how often the judge accepts the corruption. That rate is 0.201 under the plain rendering and 0.135 under the highlighted one, which indicates that the plain rendering suffered from grounding problem. The rate is an upper bound rather than an exact false-positive rate, since swapped predicate is sometimes true by coincidence. Depth. Two depths were evaluated and neither supersedes the other. The deployed graph is what each system emits when it asserts as much as its own confidence spread justifies. The matched graph is the top ten pairs of each system with no threshold, which removes length as variable: at equal depth, the number of accepted relations equals precision multiplied by depth. Why informativeness is measured rather than elicited. The judge was initially asked second question, how much relation conveys beyond what the two object names already imply, because truth alone rewards degenerate system: model answering on for most pairs is usually correct and conveys almost nothing. That question did not survive its own audit. Over the 200-image run the two questions were nearly the same axis, with (info = 0 false) = 0.998 under both renderings and (info 2 true) at 0.92 and 0.96, so rate combining them was very nearly precision multiplied by constant; and repetition went unpriced, the judge rating the baselines on relations at 1.05 on the 03 scale against 0.72 for its other predicates. The defect is not in the wording of the rubric. The redundancy of relation is property of the distribution in which it occurs, and judge shown one relation at time cannot observe that distribution. Informativeness is therefore measured as 53 surprisal, log 2 p(pred), summed over the relations the judge accepted, as in Eq. (4). Estimators. The referenced estimator uses the PSG training marginal, which is shared by both systems, so neither is scored against its own habits, and restricted to the 56 predicates both emit, so no smoothing constant affects the comparison; the out-of-vocabulary mass is reported alongside and never folded in. Tab. 7 reports the restricted-vocabulary arm, the like-for-like comparison. An open-vocabulary arm was run as control for vocabulary breadth: at matched depth the judge accepts its relations at the same rate, and it reaches 22.6 reference-free bits per image against 16.0. Since 73% of its predicates fall outside the reference, Eq. (4) cannot be evaluated for it without smoothing constant determining the comparison, and it is excluded rather than scored on biased subsample. The reference-free estimator is KrichevskyTrofimov [Krichevsky and Trofimov, 1981] description length over each systems own stream of accepted predicates: the first on is expensive and the five-hundredth nearly free, and the code charges for vocabulary size, which answers the objection that larger predicate list creates headroom by itself. It is stable in the threshold at which rare predicates are pooled, yielding 25.0 / 24.8 / 23.7 bits per image for the restricted arm over merge thresholds of 1, 3 and 10 occurrences against 7.2 for the baseline at all three, and at matched depth 16.0 against 8.0. It therefore agrees with Eq. (4) on the ordering, at slightly wider ratio. The same asymmetry appears without any judge or reference, in the predicate distributions themselves: entropy 4.00 against 2.14, and 1.9 distinct accepted predicates per graph against 1.5. Tab. 7 reports none of these, because the axis is defined as Eq. (4) and table of competing estimators would invite the reader to choose one. Normalisation. Eq. (4) is unbounded, so Tab. 3 and Fig. 1 divide it by the same quantity evaluated on the ground-truth relations of the same images, which yields the share of the information human annotator recorded that system delivers. Two properties bound this reading. The ground truth counts every annotated relation, including those whose endpoints the shared detector never found, so both systems carry the detectors recall identically and the denominator does not depend on its operating point. And the ratio can exceed one because the annotation is sparse: at deployed depth our model reaches 1.03, asserting 18.3 relations per image against 6.33 in the annotation and being credited for true relations that were never annotated. The matched-depth figure, at which both systems are below one, is the one reported.

On the released ladder, S+ costs +15% parameters and yields +7.4%, whereas S+ costs +114% parameters, 1.33 memory and 1.22 wall-clock time and yields 0.1%; the largest tower does not outperform the released one. On the zero-shot ladder the middle rung is the weakest of the three, 1.5% below S, before recovers +3.1%. Three observations matter more than the ordering. Spatial axis. On both ladders ViT-S/16+ is the best of the three on A6, and ViT-B is worse than model of less than half its size. This is the deciding evidence for the supervision-ceiling reading of 6.6: capacity cannot substitute for supervision that is absent. Source of the evidence. The lesion ladder of Tab. 10, run at all three sizes  (Fig. 28)  , shows that dependence on box geometry decreases with size (from 35.2% to 9.8% on VG150) while dependence on pixels increases (from 53.0% to 58.1%), monotonically and in all three sources. The two move in opposite directions, which rules out the simpler explanation that larger models are more robust to any lesion. Larger backbones recover from pixels what smaller ones read from 63 explicit box coordinates: substitution rather than an addition, and consistent with the training dynamics of Fig. 29. Deployment. Run through the deployment path, with detector boxes, its own calibration fit and its own count-matched threshold, the two larger towers tie, and S+ achieves the higher value on the only precision we can measure against adjudicated negatives (0.903 against 0.893). Benchmark recall reads 50 ranked slots per image, whereas the operating point emits 57 edges, about 70% of which fall on boxes that no ground-truth object matches. The capacity advantage therefore lies in part of the ranking that deployment never emits, which is the evidence behind the choice of tower in 8.1. 64 Figure 30 The recipe ladder: every arm with complete axis set, ordered by composite. sections.title: H Ablations and negative results
sections.content: H.1 Selection protocol and reproducibility Because full-scale arm costs several GPU-hours, the recipe was developed on 50k-image proxy of the corpus and promoted according to criteria fixed in advance. The reliability of that proxy is itself measured result. Its ranking of arms settles early: on the selection metric, the sign of the difference between two arms agrees with the twelve-epoch outcome for 8286% of the comparisons that exceed the noise floor, at every epoch from the first. Its levels do not settle, the composite of the winning arm rising from 0.339 on the proxy to 0.371 at full scale. The noise floor between seed-matched reruns is 1.3%, and every difference reported in this paper should be read against it. Two properties of the selection are worth stating, because both could have biased the outcome. The recipe was chosen on composite over A1, A2, A3 and A6, before A4 and A5 were defined. Recomputing every selection decision on the A1/A2/A4/A6 composite changes no outcome: the same three towers pass, the same one is released, and the backbone-learning-rate comparison still resolves to the default arm, by 0.012 OVS-F1 against +0.003 threshold where the earlier composite gave 0.006. The selection is therefore not an artefact of which axes are summed. Selection also reads the final epoch rather than the best one, which predicts out-of-distribution behaviour better ( 8.1) and inverts the ordering of some arms, including the comparison between backbone adaptation schemes. H.2 Attributions The following attributions come from the ladder of Fig. 30 and Tab. 30, each from single-variable arm against matched control, and should be read against the 1.3% noise floor. Sigmoid auxiliary: moves the projective spatial band at small transfer cost, and makes the scale of the output head trainable. Deformable scene read: improves every axis and recovers the transfer cost of the sigmoid auxiliary; the two together constitute the full-scale recipe. Layer-normalised feature taps: free, and equivalent to multi-level read costing 3 as much, which was therefore not adopted. Multi-scale sampling: +3.7% on the development composite with 9 of 11 cells improving, and regulariser rather than resolution effect: it reduces the proxys trainvalidation gap by 60%, so its gain at full scale is correspondingly smaller, as that mechanism predicts. Same-predicate feature mixing: +10.1% zero-shot tail mean recall, reproduced with two seeds, whereas the identical mechanism with random partners yields 2.8%. The classconditional matching rather than the mixing is the mechanism; both mixing arms have lower training loss than the control, which rules out an augmentation effect and points to prototype smoothing. 66 Source-aware negative masking: +12% on the spatial axis when corpora of different annotation scope are mixed ( B.1), and the best composite of the family. H.3 prior violation traced to one loss term One diagnostic is reported here because no axis of 5 can detect it. The corpus teaches that person wears bounded set of garments attached to their body. Under gated variant of the background-suppression term, the trained model violated that prior 22 more often than its training data does, asserting wearing between disjoint boxes at rate of 11.04%. Three explanations were tested and rejected. vocabulary explanation fails, since 85% of the type errors involve body parts absent from the source ontology, so the model is not choosing incorrectly among available categories. graph-reasoning explanation fails, since the fan-in is 97% co-reference, that is, the same garment attributed to several boxes of one person, which requires no relational inference. spatial-shortcut explanation fails in the opposite direction, since probes show that the entity features already identify body parts correctly, with 66.9% assigned to the correct family. Removing the gate reduced the disjoint-box wearing rate to 0.00% at no cost elsewhere, and the released model does not use it. None of A1A3 could have detected this failure, because the benchmarks own annotation never asserts the violated pairs in either direction. Checking models output against prior stated by its training data is an inexpensive measurement that is not currently made. They are reproduced in full because the calibration study that selected them, coverage over verify-before-assert, can only be interpreted against the actual text. J.1 Semantic pass You are precise visual scene analyst. Extract visually grounded relationships between the {n} , objects marked with coloured numbered dots in the image. Objects (number label): {object_list} Follow these steps carefully: STEP 1 -- Observe what each object IS DOING: Before reasoning about pairs, note the activity, , state, or role of every object. What is it doing? (grazing, running, sitting, flying, eating, carrying load, casting shadow, etc.) , What is it interacting with in the scene? (the ground, another object, person, food, etc.) STEP 2 -- For each pair, find the MOST INFORMATIVE relationship: Priority order -- stop at the first that applies: (a) Activity / locomotion -- what is one object doing relative to the other or its environment? Open vocabulary: use any precise verb phrase (grazing on, eating from, running across, standing on, walking through, casting shadow on, drinking from, pecking at, chasing, herding, pulling, pushing, swimming in, flying over, climbing, digging in ...) (b) Physical interaction -- direct manipulation, support, containment: holding, wearing, riding, carrying, sitting on, resting on, leaning against, attached to, part of, mounted on, hanging from, covering, surrounding, inside (c) Directed attention / social: looking at, watching, talking to, pointing at, following, leading Critical rules: DO NOT output any spatial or directional predicate -- spatial layout will be handled separately , Prefer open-vocabulary action phrases: describe WHAT objects are doing, not WHERE they are Use DIRECT predicates -- no "is", "are", "was", "were" prefix Each (subject_id, object_id) pair may appear AT MOST ONCE in your output STEP 3 -- Select relations: Aim for 6-10 relations total -- quality over quantity Every numbered object should appear in at least one relation If an object genuinely has no informative relation to any other marked object, skip it DO NOT pad with spatial or directional predicates STRICTLY BANNED predicates -- your output is invalid if you use any of these: has, near, next to, alongside, by, with, on, beside, and, same scene, overlapping, adjacent, associated, related, interacts, features, involves, appears, is positioned, is situated, is located, faces, supporting, displaying, above, below, behind, in front of, to the left of, to the right of, between, standing behind, standing in front of, standing beside, standing next to, sitting behind, sitting in front of, sitting beside, parked behind, parked in front of, parked beside, walking behind, walking in front of, flying above, hanging above, positioned, located, placed, arranged, oriented 71 STEP 4 -- Output: After your reasoning, output single JSON block with no extra text outside it: ```json {{"relations": [{{"subject_id": <int>, "subject_label": "<str>", "predicate": "<str>", , ``` "object_id": <int>, "object_label": "<str>"}}]}} J.2 Grow pass Here is an image and PARTIAL scene graph for it -- relationships already found between the , numbered objects. Any action, physical contact, support, use, or attention you can see that is not yet listed. Rules: Output ONLY NEW relationships. Do NOT repeat any relationship already in the list, and do NOT output the inverse of one already there. Use the MOST PRECISE open-vocabulary predicate; direct form (no "is/are"); never use vague words (near, next to, with, on alone, has, positioned, located, situated). Choose the pairs whose arrangement best DEFINES the scene's layout, most informative first.
